content: It includes citations for studies on hypertension, COVID-19, pharmacological treatments, and other related topics. 1. Independent prescribers have been studied to understand the perspectives of patients regarding their care. This research was published in Family Practice in 2010, highlighting the importance of patient-centered approaches in prescribing practices. 2. Stewart DC and colleagues explored the views of patients on pharmacist supplementary prescribing in Scotland. Their findings, published in Pharmacy World & Science in 2008, provide insights into the role of pharmacists in collaborative healthcare models. 3. Jacob V and co-authors conducted a systematic review on the economics of team-based care in managing blood pressure. Their work, published in American Journal of Preventive Medicine in 2015, emphasizes the cost-effectiveness of collaborative care models in hypertension management. 4. Kulchaitanaroaj P and colleagues performed a cost-utility analysis comparing physician-pharmacist collaborative interventions for hypertension treatment with usual care. Their study, published in Journal of Hypertension in 2017, demonstrated the economic and clinical benefits of such collaborative approaches. 5. Keasley J and co-authors systematically reviewed the burden of hypertension, access to healthcare services, and patient perspectives in humanitarian crisis settings. Their findings, published in BMJ Global Health in 2020, underscore the challenges faced by vulnerable populations in managing hypertension. 6. Sekkarie M and colleagues discussed the challenges and potential solutions for managing end-stage kidney disease in areas affected by armed conflicts. Their work, published in Seminars in Nephrology in 2020, highlights the critical need for innovative healthcare delivery in conflict zones. 7. Al-Makki A and co-authors described the response of the Syrian National Kidney Foundation to the needs of kidney patients during the Syrian crisis. Their report, published in Avicenna Journal of Medicine in 2014, illustrates the importance of local initiatives in addressing healthcare gaps during emergencies. 8. Jawad M and colleagues conducted a systematic review on the impact of armed conflict on cardiovascular disease risk. Their study, published in Heart in 2019, provides evidence of the long-term health consequences of conflict on cardiovascular health. 9. Howard JT and co-authors investigated the association between initial injury severity, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and long-term hypertension risk in combat-injured individuals. Their findings, published in Hypertension in 2018, reveal the interplay between physical and psychological trauma and chronic disease development. 10. Doocy S and colleagues characterized Syrian and Lebanese patients with diabetes and hypertension in Lebanon. Their study, published in Open Hypertension Journal in 2018, highlights the healthcare needs of displaced populations in host countries. 11. Sun X-C and co-authors examined the clinical characteristics of hypertension among victims in temporary shelters following the Wenchuan earthquake in China. Their research, published in European Review for Medical and Pharmacological Sciences in 2013, sheds light on the health challenges faced by disaster-affected populations. 12. Kario K discussed the unique characteristics, mechanisms, and management strategies for disaster-related hypertension. This work, published in Circulation Journal in 2012, emphasizes the need for tailored approaches to hypertension care during emergencies. 13. Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) published clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of various conditions, including hypertension, in 2013. These guidelines serve as a critical resource for healthcare providers in resource-limited settings. 14. The World Health Organization (WHO) provided guidance on emergency health kits and pharmacological treatments for hypertension, accessible through their official website as of March 2021. 15. Richardson S and colleagues analyzed the presenting characteristics, comorbidities, and outcomes of 5,700 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 in the New York City area. Their findings, published in JAMA in 2020, offer valuable insights into the clinical course of COVID-19 in hospitalized patients. 16. Xie J and co-authors described the clinical characteristics of patients who died from COVID-19 in China. Their study, published in JAMA Network Open in 2020, highlights the factors associated with poor outcomes in severe cases. 17. Hoffmann M and colleagues demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 cell entry depends on ACE2 and TMPRSS2 and can be blocked by a clinically proven protease inhibitor. Their research, published in Cell, provides a foundation for therapeutic interventions targeting viral entry mechanisms. 18. Vaduganathan M and co-authors reviewed the use of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors in patients with COVID-19. Their work, published in New England Journal of Medicine in 2020, addresses concerns about the safety and efficacy of these medications during the pandemic. 19. Sparks MA and colleagues discussed the role of ACE2 in hypertension and its implications for COVID-19. Their findings, accessible online, contribute to the understanding of the intersection between hypertension and infectious diseases. 20. Kompotiatis P and Garovic VD reviewed the diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes of hypertensive disorders during pregnancy. Their chapter in a case-based approach to hypertension, published in 2020, provides practical guidance for managing these conditions. 21. Kuklina EV and co-authors analyzed the association between hypertensive disorders and severe obstetric morbidity in the United States. Their study, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology in 2009, highlights the significant impact of hypertension on maternal health. 22. Creanga AA and colleagues examined pregnancy-related mortality in the United States from 2006 to 2010. Their findings, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology in 2015, underscore the need for improved maternal healthcare services. 23. Abalos E and co-authors conducted a Cochrane systematic review on antihypertensive drug therapy for mild to moderate hypertension during pregnancy. Their review, published in 2018, provides evidence-based recommendations for managing hypertension in pregnant women. 24. The WHO acknowledged the contributions of various experts and organizations in developing guidelines for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults. These guidelines were created through a collaborative process involving systematic reviews, external peer reviews, and expert consultations.
